title: The Rising Rate

scenario.situation: The fraud rate per active user jumped from 0.8% to 1.3% this month — a 63% relative increase.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The risk team assumes fraudsters got more active and wants to tighten transaction rules immediately.
scenario.question: Did fraud actually surge, or is something else driving the rate increase?

decisions.prompt: The risk team is ready to escalate. How do you frame your investigation before touching any fraud data?

options.label: Audit the fraud detection pipeline
options.detail: Check whether the detection model or rules changed this month, which could inflate flagged cases.
options.consequence: The pipeline looks clean — no rule changes, no model retraining. You've ruled out one thing but spent time on a dead end, and you still don't know why the rate moved.
options.divergenceCost: Looked for a technical artifact before decomposing the metric itself.

options.label: Decompose the rate into numerator and denominator trends separately
options.detail: Before assuming fraud grew, chart absolute fraud counts and active-user counts independently to see which component moved.
options.consequence: Plotting both series immediately reveals the divergence: fraud counts are flat while active users dropped sharply. The rate rose because the base shrank — a finding the risk team's framing would never surface.

options.label: Segment fraud cases by attack vector
options.detail: Break down fraud by type — account takeover, card not present, synthetic identity — to find which vector spiked.
options.consequence: No single vector shows a meaningful spike. You've sliced a flat numerator into smaller flat pieces and produced noise, not signal.
options.divergenceCost: Assumed the numerator drove the move and segmented before verifying it changed at all.

options.label: Compare this month's fraud rate to the same month last year
options.detail: Use a year-over-year view to control for seasonality.
options.consequence: The YoY rate is also elevated — but last year's denominator was different too. You've added a second confounded comparison without resolving the first.
options.divergenceCost: Reached for a benchmark comparison before understanding what the current rate is actually measuring.

decisions.prompt: You decide to inspect the components. Which metric view do you bring to the team to confirm what actually moved?

artifact.title: Fraud rate per active user — last 3 months
artifact.caption: The rate jumped sharply this month. Is the problem in the numerator, the denominator, or both?

options.label: Fraud rate trend over time
options.detail: Show the month-over-month fraud rate chart — the same number that triggered the alert.
options.consequence: The chart confirms the rate rose, but it still doesn't tell you whether fraud counts climbed or active users fell. You're presenting the question, not the answer.
options.divergenceCost: Re-presented the alerting metric without decomposing it — the original confusion remains intact.

options.label: Side-by-side absolute counts: fraud events vs. active users
options.detail: Plot raw fraud event counts and raw active-user counts on the same time axis so both components are visible.
options.consequence: The picture is unambiguous: fraud event counts have been flat for three months while active users dropped by 38% this month following a churn event. The rate rise is entirely denominator-driven — there is no fraud surge.

artifact.title: Absolute fraud events vs. active users — last 3 months
artifact.caption: Fraud counts are flat. Active users fell 38% after a churn event. The denominator collapse — not a fraud surge — drove the rate increase.

decisions.prompt: The data shows flat fraud counts and a collapsed active-user base. What do you tell the risk team?

options.label: "There is no fraud surge — the rate moved because users churned. Stand down."
options.detail: Make the definitive call and recommend no action.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified the denominator effect, but standing down entirely is premature. The churn event changed your user mix, which could expose new fraud patterns going forward. Confidence without a forward-looking check leaves a real risk unmonitored.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and skipped a forward-looking risk check after a major base change.

options.label: "The rate rise appears denominator-driven — fraud counts are flat and active users dropped 38%. Tightening rules now would likely be premature, but we should monitor absolute fraud counts closely over the next cycle and assess whether the new user mix carries different risk characteristics."
options.detail: Report the finding, flag the limit of the analysis, and propose a monitoring path.
options.consequence: You've reframed the alert with evidence, prevented a potentially harmful rule change, and built in a credible forward check. The risk team gets a clear, defensible answer with a responsible next step.

insight: Fraud didn't surge — the active-user base shrank 38% after a churn event, and the flat numerator divided by a smaller denominator produced the alarming rate. The lesson is structural: any rate metric can move because its denominator moved, entirely independent of the phenomenon you think you're measuring. Before investigating why a rate changed, verify which component — numerator or denominator — actually changed, and by how much.
